key_finding: Broad survey of DC plan design finding automatic enrollment and default investment options carry both short-term participation gains and potential negative effects on longer-term participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative literature overview covering plan design research, financial literacy heterogeneity, and recent policy changes (SECURE 2.0). Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a synthesis view of the engagement-cost side of default enrollment that echoes the support team's objection, but every finding is from employer-sponsored 401(k) research so it can only frame the question, not answer it for our product.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan setting, not consumer self-directed
narrative overview rather than a systematic review, so no pooled effect sizes
relevance_reason: Provides broad context on default-driven engagement trade-offs in the closest analogous literature.

key_finding: Accounting for job separation, withdrawal on separation, and opt-out from auto-escalation, steady-state savings increase only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation, far smaller than headline estimates; only 40% of defaulted employees escalate on the first scheduled date.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, vesting, and opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's objection: the enrolment lift from a default is real but its dollar impact erodes once realistic attrition and disengagement are modeled, which is exactly the persistence question the brief asks about.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer intermediary and vesting mechanics that do not carry over to a consumer app
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults straightforwardly translate into more saving once medium-run dynamics are modeled.

key_finding: A field experiment nudging cardholders off minimum-payment autopay reduced minimum-only payments by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders chose autopay amounts barely above the minimum and manual payments fell.
methodology: Randomized field experiment on credit card autopay enrollment defaults, six-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt levels.
why_it_matters: Shows in a genuinely consumer, self-directed financial-app setting that changing the enrolment default shifts nominal behavior without changing the underlying financial outcome — the exact 'vanity metric' risk the brief raises for round-up enrolment.
limitations: credit card repayment behavior differs from voluntary savings accumulation
liquidity constraints specific to indebted cardholders may not generalize to savers
relevance_reason: Consumer fintech evidence that a default/nudge changed enrolment status without changing the amount that matters, directly bearing on the enrolment-vs-amount question.

key_finding: Nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most affected individuals later actively opted out, and the effect was stronger when incentives were high and knowledge of enrollment status was low.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around a nationwide auto-enrollment policy change.
why_it_matters: Gives a large, clean, recent default-effect size and shows the effect depends on incentive strength and awareness, both factors we can vary in the round-up design, though the setting is a public pension, not a self-directed app.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a consumer financial app
enrollees are low-income government scheme participants rather than self-selecting app users
relevance_reason: Recent, large-sample quantification of an opt-out default effect and its moderators, useful as an upper-bound benchmark.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, are markedly attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings increases though a meaningful reduction in savings inequality, and a life-cycle model implies a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel analysis of over 100 US retirement plans and a UK representative panel, complemented by a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's persistence question: default enrolment effects on amount, not just headcount, shrink substantially between 12 and 36 months, which should temper any enrolment-lift argument used to justify opt-out.
limitations: retirement savings plans with locked/illiquid balances, unlike a liquid round-up pot
employer-plan intermediary context absent in a banking app
relevance_reason: Best available quantification of how default-driven savings gains decay over the medium run, the central persistence question in the brief.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term participation and coverage but induces behavioral inertia — low default contribution rates, inactive account management, and account churn — such that participation alone does not demonstrate a welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative policy review of default enrollment research in US retirement plans. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: States explicitly, as a policy argument rather than a single study, the mechanism our support team worries about: passive enrollees stay at defaults and disengage, so raw enrolment numbers overstate benefit.
limitations: US retirement plan policy commentary, not consumer fintech
narrative/policy piece rather than a study with its own data or effect sizes
relevance_reason: Directly frames the 'passive trap' concern central to the brief's internal debate, even though set in retirement plans.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a 5-country sample (n=4207), defaults significantly shifted risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default nudge lowered users' rating of the advisor, especially when the targeted default was refused, and framing of the default question itself had smaller but measurable anchoring effects.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large multi-country representative sample, manipulating default presence and framing in an investment-risk context.
why_it_matters: Directly informs whether a pre-set multiplier reads as helpful or manipulative: it shows a default can move behavior while simultaneously damaging trust when overridden, which should weigh heavily on the entry-mechanism decision under EU dark-pattern scrutiny.
limitations: wealth-manager investment advice context rather than a savings-pot multiplier
effect on trust/rating measured immediately, not over 6-12 months of app use
relevance_reason: Consumer financial-advice setting showing both the anchoring power and the reputational cost of defaults, central to the entry-design trade-off.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but roughly 80% of participants accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, and half still had not moved off the default rate/fund after three years, roughly offsetting participation gains against depressed savings and investment quality.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking automatic enrollment effects on participation, contribution rate, and asset allocation over three years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors the great majority of users for years, which is exactly the mechanism the brief worries about for a pre-selected round-up multiplier — this is the study the newer literature answers.
limitations: 401(k) employer-sponsored plan, not a consumer app
no year listed and very dated relative to the app/liquidity/regulatory context the brief flags as having changed
relevance_reason: Foundational anchoring evidence on pre-set default levels that the level-design decision must be measured against.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost together (friction complementarity), and adding a 15% tip option to the existing 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of achievable welfare gain at 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million consumer transactions, validated against an independent stated-preference survey of true preferences.
why_it_matters: Offers a directly transferable method for the level-design decision: it shows preset menu options anchor choices largely through friction rather than preference change, and quantifies how adding/removing a preset option shifts welfare — precisely the multiplier-menu question the brief poses.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings accumulation
single transaction context rather than repeated app engagement over months
relevance_reason: Genuine consumer, self-directed setting with a structural model of preset-menu anchoring directly applicable to the multiplier design choice.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default choice architecture produces lasting versus fading downstream effects on consumer behavior, identifying time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
methodology: Conceptual review and framework synthesis of the consumer behavior literature on default effects. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the project a structured way to decide what to measure at 6-12 months (retention, amount, disengagement) rather than only enrolment, directly shaping the measurement plan for whichever entry design is chosen.
limitations: theoretical/taxonomic rather than an empirical estimate
not specific to financial products, so moderators require validation in the app context
relevance_reason: A recent synthesis of exactly the persistence-and-depth question the brief raises, useful for designing what to track post-launch.

key_finding: Characterizes optimal default design as an asymptotic solution, showing that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, some form of weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions for externalities and normative disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical economic model with asymptotic characterization and numerical simulations verifying approximation accuracy.
why_it_matters: Offers a general normative argument for when minimizing opt-out (i.e., an opt-out enrolment default) is the theoretically optimal choice-architecture design, relevant background for justifying the entry-mechanism decision, but it names no concrete population or product.
limitations: pure theoretical model with no empirical population or setting
normative optimum depends on assumptions about designer-chooser value agreement that are untested here
relevance_reason: General theory of optimal defaults bearing on the opt-in/opt-out/active-choice decision, though abstracted from any real setting.

key_finding: An opt-in payroll-deduction short-term (liquid, withdraw-anytime) savings program at five UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate an account, but among those who did, 96% still held a balance and 87% received a payroll contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of program introduction and take-up/retention tracked over the first 12 months post-activation at five UK employers.
why_it_matters: The closest available analogue to a liquid round-up product: shows opt-in take-up for a liquid, flexible savings account can be vanishingly low even though committed users are highly persistent, informing the entry-mechanism trade-off directly.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction intermediary rather than an independent banking app user
take-up sample of adopters may be highly self-selected, limiting persistence generalizability
relevance_reason: Directly studies opt-in enrolment and 12-month persistence for a liquid, withdrawable savings product, the nearest real-world analogue to round-up savings.

key_finding: Maps EU laws addressing dark patterns (including default pre-selection) and develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, arguing EU regulation of dark patterns is fundamentally about protecting consumer decision-making autonomy.
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy construction based on EU consumer protection law. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the concrete legal/regulatory framework for judging whether an opt-out round-up default with pre-selected multiplier would read as a dark pattern under EU law, directly informing the reputational-risk half of the entry and level decisions.
limitations: legal/doctrinal analysis, not an empirical behavioral study
does not measure actual consumer perception or enrolment/persistence outcomes
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern and manipulation-risk framing the brief flags as a reputational concern for an opt-out default.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D produce large, persistent enrollment and drug-utilization effects, and beneficiary passivity remains high even when the default option causes substantial financial loss.
methodology: Two natural experiments plus a third exploiting random assignment to default options and random transitory shocks to active-choice attentiveness; large administrative sample of low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Shows default effects can be extremely persistent and insensitive to the value of the default — a caution that our opt-out design could enrol people who never revisit their setting even when a different multiplier would clearly serve them better, and that active-choice variation may reflect noise rather than genuine engagement.
limitations: health-insurance plan choice, not a consumer financial/savings product
government-administered program rather than a self-directed banking app
relevance_reason: Directly tests default effect size, persistence, and the active-choice mechanism, all named in the brief's core questions, in a large individual-choice (non-employer) setting.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees remained at the default after 12 months (versus roughly half at lower defaults elsewhere), and many stayed at a rate that was suboptimal given the employer match.
methodology: Administrative data analysis of a single retirement plan's unusually high default, benchmarked against a literature review of lower-default plans; abstract-only detail on mechanism.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that a preset level anchors people onto a possibly-wrong number — the core worry behind our multiplier pre-selection choice — and that anchoring is stronger for lower-income users, exactly the distributional risk the brief flags.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed banking app
abstract gives limited detail on mechanism
relevance_reason: The clearest available evidence on whether a preset default level anchors the ultimately-chosen contribution amount, one of the two open design decisions.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment sharply raised participation, and most auto-enrolled employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation, a combination almost no one chose under opt-in.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment at a single large U.S. corporation comparing cohorts hired under opt-in versus automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that people read a default as implicit advice — the same dynamic our pre-selected multiplier risks triggering — but it predates smartphone banking, liquid savings, and current EU default-transparency norms, so it sets a ceiling rather than a direct answer.
limitations: 2001 employer 401(k) study, not a consumer app
locked retirement savings rather than liquid, withdrawable funds
no long-horizon persistence or withdrawal data
relevance_reason: The classic 'power of suggestion' result that today's default-effect and anchoring literature, including several other shortlisted papers, is responding to or extending.

key_finding: Abstract text was not retrievable; title and authorship indicate field experiments on automating short-term, liquid payroll savings across four large U.K. programs.
methodology: abstract-only (text corrupted in the record); reportedly large-scale U.K. field experiments led by researchers known for automatic-enrollment savings work.
why_it_matters: If it holds what the title promises, this is the closest available analog to our product — short-term, liquid, automated savings rather than locked retirement funds — but the missing abstract means we cannot yet extract effect sizes to act on.
limitations: abstract not retrievable, so key numbers are unknown
payroll-mediated savings may still involve an employer-like intermediary, which the brief says does not carry over cleanly
relevance_reason: Title and setting (short-term liquid payroll savings, U.K. field experiments) match the brief's population and outcome concerns more closely than most other shortlisted work, but content could not be verified from the abstract given.

key_finding: No abstract was available; the title indicates a comparison of savings behavior between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined-contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only; no substantive content available.
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant to the enrolment-design question, but nothing in the record lets us judge whether it adds any effect size or mechanism beyond what other automatic-enrollment studies already show.
limitations: abstract missing entirely, no verifiable findings
employer-sponsored retirement plan setting, not a consumer app
relevance_reason: Title-level match to the automatic-vs-voluntary enrollment question, but there is no substantive content to weigh.

key_finding: At-scale U.K. bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though consumers still capture less than half of the available savings.
methodology: Multiple large-scale field experiments run directly inside major U.K. retail banks, with market-wide extrapolation of savings.
why_it_matters: The nearest real-world precedent to our exact decision: automatic (opt-out-style) enrollment into a discretionary consumer-banking feature, run at scale inside a bank, with real behavior-change effect sizes — strong evidence that opt-out can produce durable, economically meaningful benefit rather than just nominal sign-up, while also showing the benefit captured is only partial, which should temper how much we claim from enrolment numbers alone.
limitations: overdraft alerts, not a savings/round-up feature specifically
effect measured as charges avoided rather than savings-pot balances or long-term retention
relevance_reason: Same institutional setting (consumer retail banking app, U.K.), same design lever (automatic enrollment vs. opt-in), with real effect sizes on realized benefit, not just enrolment counts.

key_finding: Limited trust in financial institutions and minority/non-national status are each associated with both under-saving and early withdrawal of retirement savings, putting the same people at risk on both sides of the saving decision.
methodology: Analysis of three nationally representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) surrounding a policy reform introducing an early pension withdrawal option.
why_it_matters: Speaks directly to the support team's disengagement/withdrawal worry and to who is harmed: it treats the psychology of early withdrawal as distinct from the psychology of under-saving, which is exactly the split our round-up product needs to understand before assuming enrolment numbers translate into retained savings.
limitations: mandatory/quasi-mandatory pension system, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
Estonian institutional-trust context may not generalize to our regulatory environment
relevance_reason: Directly addresses persistence/withdrawal and distributional harm — who is helped versus hurt by savings defaults — a core open question in the brief.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' (an extra sign-up step) to a health-insurance auto-enrollment policy cut enrollment by 33% and differentially excluded younger, healthier, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Policy natural experiment studying removal/addition of an auto-enrollment step, combined with a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Shows that even 'minor' friction of the kind an opt-in or active-choice design imposes can produce large, regressive drop-off — directly relevant to whether opt-in or active choice would disproportionately exclude exactly the users the round-up feature might most help.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a consumer savings product
enrollment effect studied, not downstream engagement or amount saved
relevance_reason: Quantifies how enrollment friction, the mechanism behind opt-in/active-choice, can regressively exclude vulnerable users, feeding directly into the brief's distributional question.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, people reported being less likely to get a vaccine booster when told they would be automatically enrolled, and reflecting on the default further reduced both intentions and policy approval.
methodology: Large-scale multi-country online survey experiment manipulating disclosure/reflection about a hypothetical default-enrollment policy.
why_it_matters: Directly challenges the 'defaults always help, and passively' premise: making a default salient can itself trigger backlash and reduce approval, which matters for whether our opt-out design should be disclosed prominently, as EU transparency norms would push, without undermining the effect or reading as a dark pattern.
limitations: vaccination policy, not a financial product
hypothetical/stated-intention survey design rather than revealed behavior
relevance_reason: Contradicts the assumption that defaults are neutrally accepted, showing transparency about a default can itself change behavior and support — central to the EU dark-pattern reputational risk the brief raises.

key_finding: Following the randomized U.K. roll-out of pension automatic enrollment to about 160,000 small employers, each additional month raised average pension savings by £32-38 but also raised unsecured debt by £7 and mortgage balances by £118, though it lowered loan defaults and modestly raised credit scores.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment exploiting the staggered, effectively randomized roll-out of U.K. automatic enrollment across small employers, tracked over 41 months.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's question of whether defaults change real financial position or just nominal enrollment: nominal savings gains here are partly offset by additional borrowing, a caution against treating an enrolment or pot-balance number as a clean welfare win.
limitations: employer-sponsored pension automatic enrollment, not a consumer app feature
locked pension savings rather than liquid, withdrawable round-up savings
relevance_reason: Long-horizon (41-month) evidence that automatic-enrollment savings gains can be partially offset by other financial behavior, directly informing the amount-saved-versus-nominal-enrolment question and offering a contradicting data point against 'defaults are a pure win.'

key_finding: Among Millennials, auto-enrollment and employer-matching provisions are associated with a higher likelihood of retirement-plan participation, controlling for debt, income, and risk tolerance.
methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study.
why_it_matters: Adds another correlational confirmation that auto-enrollment associates with higher participation, but offers no new mechanism, persistence, anchoring, or distributional detail beyond what stronger experimental papers in this set already establish.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer product
correlational survey design, not causal
relevance_reason: Marginally on-topic (auto-enrollment and participation) but adds little beyond confirming the direction of the well-established default effect.

key_finding: Across six OECD countries with voluntary-pension auto-enrolment, coverage exceeds 50% except in Türkiye, and flat-rate subsidies produce more even coverage across income groups than tax exemptions, which favor higher earners.
methodology: Comparative multi-country case-study analysis of policy design, incentives, and institutional environment.
why_it_matters: Illustrates at a macro/policy level that the structure of accompanying incentives shapes who benefits from a default, echoing the brief's distributional concern, but it operates at country-policy scale rather than app-level choice architecture.
limitations: national pension-policy scale, not individual product design
voluntary pension pillar, not a liquid consumer savings feature
case-study/comparative method rather than a controlled effect-size estimate
relevance_reason: Provides cross-country evidence on how incentive and default design shape distributional participation outcomes, tangential background to the brief's who-is-helped question.

key_finding: A preregistered scoping review of 16 studies finds online gambling platforms use dark patterns including high defaults on stake, deposit, and reality-check settings and unnecessary friction to close accounts, though evidence on behavioral impact remains sparse.
methodology: Preregistered scoping review with systematic database and grey-literature search, mapped to a transdisciplinary dark-pattern framework.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, reviewed taxonomy of when a default reads as manipulative (e.g., high stake/deposit defaults, exit friction) rather than helpful — exactly the line our EU consumer-protection context requires us to stay on the right side of when choosing multiplier defaults and exit flows.
limitations: online gambling platforms, not a savings or banking product
review authors note behavioral-impact evidence is itself sparse and fragmented
relevance_reason: The only review in the shortlist directly addressing when a default is perceived as a dark pattern, a reputational risk the brief explicitly flags.

key_finding: Consumers across all demographic groups are susceptible to dark patterns regardless of income, education, or age, but requiring an active payment action (friction) significantly reduces dark-pattern effectiveness.
methodology: Novel empirical/experimental design testing dark pattern exposure and susceptibility across consumer groups; abstract-only detail on sample.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the entry-design choice: it shows that removing friction (single-click, no confirming action) is exactly what makes manipulative defaults most effective, which argues against a frictionless opt-out and toward active-choice or a confirmable opt-out under EU DSA scrutiny.
limitations: general digital markets setting, not specifically a savings/fintech product
abstract does not quantify effect sizes numerically
relevance_reason: Gives EU-regulatory-relevant evidence on when a default becomes a dark pattern and how required action mitigates that, bearing directly on the entry-mechanism decision.

key_finding: 68% of users unaware of dark patterns picked the service-promoted expensive plan under confirmshaming versus 35% among knowledgeable users; knowledge of the tactic makes people more likely to reject the promoted default choice.
methodology: Experimental manipulation of confirmshaming vs trick-question dark patterns on a mock subscription streaming site; abstract-only sample detail.
why_it_matters: Shows user sophistication moderates susceptibility to promoted-choice patterns, relevant to whether a pre-set multiplier could be read as a nudge toward a higher tier, but the setting is a streaming subscription, not a savings tool.
limitations: streaming subscription context, not financial savings
no measure of enrollment persistence or amount saved over time
relevance_reason: Analogous evidence on how promoted/default options and user sophistication interact, relevant to anchoring risk of a pre-set multiplier.

key_finding: Household income for the top 5% of health-insurance decision-makers by surplus captured is almost three times that of the bottom 5%, with education and quantitative training predicting choice quality more than income.
methodology: Population-wide administrative data on health insurance choices and utilization in the Netherlands.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that self-directed choice quality is steeply socioeconomically stratified, which bears directly on the brief's concern about who is helped versus hurt by any given enrolment/level design — those without financial sophistication may do worse under an unassisted 'blank field' level choice.
limitations: health insurance market, not a savings/round-up product
no default or opt-out manipulation studied
relevance_reason: Provides a strong distributional evidence base for the equity concern (C5) even though it is not about defaults specifically.

key_finding: Categorizes manipulative digital nudges under the FORCES framework (Frame, Obstruct, Ruse, Compel, Entangle, Seduce) and notes behavioural interventions against manipulation have mixed effects at best.
methodology: Narrative review/opinion piece synthesizing dark-pattern taxonomy; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a taxonomy for self-auditing whether the opt-out design (or a pre-selected multiplier) would read as one of the FORCES categories, useful for the EU reputational-risk question.
limitations: narrative overview, not a systematic review or empirical study
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Provides a manipulation taxonomy directly usable for assessing dark-pattern risk in the two open design decisions.

key_finding: Proposes 'behavioral audits' as a principles-based regulatory tool to distinguish beneficial choice architecture from deceptive dark patterns.
methodology: Conceptual/policy article proposing an audit methodology; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete method (behavioural audit) the team could apply to pre-check whether the chosen opt-out or preset-multiplier design would be judged manipulative before shipping.
limitations: proposal-level, not empirically tested
general digital choice architecture, not financial-product specific
relevance_reason: Offers an actionable auditing method for the manipulation-risk question central to the entry-design decision.

key_finding: Argues that behavioural policies overriding agency (e.g. automatic defaults) risk non-persistent treatment effects, compensatory spillovers, or reactance, and reviews boosts, debiasing, and nudge+ as agency-preserving alternatives.
methodology: Conceptual review comparing agency-enhancing behavioural frameworks; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly challenges the 'defaults always help' premise by tying non-persistence and backfire risk to agency-overriding designs, and frames active-choice-like mechanisms (nudge+) as a way to capture benefit without the disengagement cost.
limitations: general behavioural-public-policy theory, not consumer financial or app-specific
no empirical effect sizes
relevance_reason: Provides the theoretical counter-argument to blanket opt-out enrolment and a rationale for testing active choice as a middle path.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised campaign donations by over $43M but also increased refund requests by almost $3M, with the largest impact on small and default-inexperienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the different rollout timing of pre-checked recurring-donation boxes across 2020 US campaign websites.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world analogue to a pre-checked recurring micro-contribution default: it shows the default drives large nominal uptake but concentrates harm (regret/refunds) on smaller, less-experienced users — exactly the disengagement/complaint risk the support team is worried about for round-up enrolment.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
no 6-12 month persistence measure beyond refund requests
relevance_reason: Directly transfers the mechanism of a pre-checked recurring-payment default to the round-up feature's opt-out design, with quantified uptake and harm effects.

key_finding: A strong default effect on energy-efficient appliance choice was found in both the Philippines and the US, and manipulating trust in the choice architect did not change the size of the default effect.
methodology: Field experiments in two countries (Philippines n=909, US n=925) manipulating trust in a real-estate-agent choice architect.
why_it_matters: Shows default effects can persist even when the choice architect is not trusted, which argues that reputational concerns about the round-up default may not undermine its enrolment effect but does support calls for regulating default use responsibly.
limitations: appliance-purchase setting via a real-estate-agent intermediary, not a consumer fintech app
no persistence or amount-saved follow-up
relevance_reason: Provides evidence on the robustness of default effects independent of trust, relevant to the reputational-risk question around opt-out enrolment.

key_finding: Mobile banking apps' saving features, combined with omnichannel financial-literacy messaging, are associated with users' perceived improvement in savings, mediated by perceived usefulness and trust in the app.
methodology: Mixed-methods: six interviews, content analysis of three banking apps' saving features, and a 215-respondent survey.
why_it_matters: Confirms the exact product category (mobile banking savings features) but addresses marketing/engagement drivers rather than enrolment mechanism or level-setting design, so it does not move either open decision much.
limitations: self-reported perceived savings improvement, not measured enrolment or amounts
does not study defaults, opt-in/opt-out, or preset levels at all
relevance_reason: Matches the exact product setting (banking-app savings features) but is orthogonal to the choice-architecture decisions in question.

key_finding: Proposes that people infer organizational intent from behavioural interventions (e.g. treating a default as a recommendation), and reject defaults perceived as self-serving, which explains inconsistent intervention effects across implementations.
methodology: Conceptual framework paper synthesizing behavioural-science evidence on inferences from interventions; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a mechanism for predicting when the round-up opt-out will be read as a helpful recommendation versus a self-serving dark pattern, directly informing how the entry mechanism should be framed to preserve trust.
limitations: general organizational behaviour-change context, not consumer financial products
no empirical effect sizes, purely theoretical framework
relevance_reason: Provides the psychological mechanism behind why the same default can help or backfire depending on perceived intent, central to the manipulation-risk question.

key_finding: FTC behavioural research shows advertising-disclosure salience affects consumer recognition/engagement, and a usability-focused redesign of a complaint website changed complaint submission rates and information quality.
methodology: A laboratory experiment on disclosure salience plus a retrospective natural-experiment evaluation of a redesigned complaint website.
why_it_matters: Illustrates how a regulator empirically evaluates digital design choices for consumer protection, offering a template for pre-launch testing of the round-up feature's onboarding screens, but does not address enrolment defaults or contribution levels directly.
limitations: focus is on advertising disclosures and complaint tools, not savings enrolment or contribution defaults
US FTC regulatory context, not EU
relevance_reason: Tangentially relevant as a model of empirical consumer-protection evaluation methodology, but not on the enrolment/level question itself.

key_finding: A systematic synthesis of 66 peer-reviewed articles identifies defaults, framing, informational cues, reminders, and social norms as the dominant nudges in financial decision-making, mapping 19 antecedents, 24 decision types, and 19 outcomes, but finds evidence concentrated in narrow institutional/geographic contexts.
methodology: Systematic literature review using the SPAR-4-SLR protocol across Web of Science and Scopus, organized via ADO and TCM frameworks.
why_it_matters: This is the review/synthesis of nudges specifically in financial decision-making the brief asked for, giving a structural map of what is and isn't well studied (e.g. it flags contextual imbalance), useful for identifying where our decisions sit relative to existing evidence.
limitations: no quantitative effect sizes reported in the abstract, more a thematic/bibliometric mapping than a meta-analysis
does not isolate consumer round-up/liquid-savings products specifically
relevance_reason: Provides the requested review-level synthesis of nudges in finance, directly in the financial decision-making domain the brief targets.

key_finding: Proposes a typology of hidden costs of nudge interventions across emotional/cognitive, behavioural, social/relational, and secondary domains, arguing effectiveness does not always mean improved wellbeing.
methodology: Review-conceptual article building an empirically-grounded catalogue of behavioural-intervention costs; abstract-only, in Polish.
why_it_matters: Directly challenges the 'defaults always help' premise by cataloguing wellbeing costs (e.g. behavioural/social costs of passive enrolment) that could underlie the support team's complaint and withdrawal concerns.
limitations: general public-policy nudge context, not consumer financial products specifically
conceptual typology, not quantified effect sizes
relevance_reason: Offers a structured counter-argument and cost taxonomy relevant to weighing the enrolment-lift benefit against disengagement/complaint costs.

key_finding: Theory-informed experimental work on individuals' differential susceptibility to dark patterns in e-commerce (no abstract provided, so specifics unavailable).
methodology: abstract-only
why_it_matters: Speaks directly to the EU reputational-risk question of when a default or nudge reads as manipulative rather than helpful, which bears on whether opt-out enrolment or a pre-selected multiplier could be perceived as a dark pattern.
limitations: no abstract available, so effect sizes and design details are unknown
e-commerce setting rather than consumer financial app
unclear whether findings generalize to enrolment/level defaults specifically
relevance_reason: Directly targets the manipulation-perception question (C5) the brief flags as a reputational risk for the round-up feature.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions increase wealth accumulation substantially, while active-choice subsidies induce only 1 cent of extra saving per dollar spent because 85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies.
methodology: Administrative panel data covering the population of Denmark; quasi-experimental analysis of active vs passive savings policy responses.
why_it_matters: Sets the classic benchmark that passive/default mechanisms vastly outperform active-choice subsidies for the majority of people, which the brief's active-choice option must be measured against, but the employer-intermediary mechanism does not carry over cleanly to a self-directed banking app.
limitations: employer-mediated retirement savings, not a self-directed consumer app
locked/illiquid retirement accounts, unlike the liquid round-up product
no direct measure of anchoring on preset contribution levels
relevance_reason: The definitive large-sample evidence on default vs active-choice effect sizes and heterogeneity that the current consumer-fintech literature responds to.

key_finding: Proposes and tests 'enhanced active choice' — active choice that highlights losses from the non-preferred option — as an alternative to opt-out defaults when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical, via field experiments.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments; abstract does not report effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, testable variant of active choice (loss-framed) that could let the team capture much of the enrolment benefit without full opt-out, directly informing the entry-design decision.
limitations: health/medication-adherence context rather than consumer financial product
no quantitative effect sizes reported in the abstract
not tested in a liquid-savings or app-based setting
relevance_reason: Directly compares active choice against opt-out defaults and proposes a design refinement, matching the brief's C6 question almost exactly.

key_finding: A randomized nudge (payment reminders) in a Brazilian financial app reduced credit-card late fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%, with users who already overdraft experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Field RCT with a consumer financial management platform, administrative fee data.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's stated worry — a well-intentioned default/nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — arguing against blanket opt-out enrolment without segmentation.
limitations: studies a reminder nudge, not an enrolment default per se
credit/overdraft context rather than a savings round-up feature
Brazilian market, not EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: The clearest consumer-financial-app evidence that nudges/defaults can have distributional side effects, hurting the subgroup least equipped to benefit — exactly the heterogeneity question the brief raises.

key_finding: Randomized default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% match), driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and it also increased subsequent active saving after the study ended.
methodology: Field experiment randomly assigning employees in Afghanistan to different default savings account configurations, with mechanism-testing interventions.
why_it_matters: Identifies the psychological mechanisms (present bias, cognitive cost) behind default effects, which is useful for predicting whether an opt-out round-up default will work similarly in a mobile banking context even though the trust intermediary differs.
limitations: employer/salary-linked savings, not a self-directed consumer app
developing-country context far from EU regulatory setting
does not report amounts saved or retention past the study window in detail
relevance_reason: Provides mechanistic evidence for why defaults move enrolment, relevant to predicting default persistence and behavior change even outside the employer setting.

key_finding: A synthesis of household finance evidence covering consumption/savings, borrowing, payments, and asset allocation, alongside interventions including choice architecture and product design used by firms and governments to shape financial behavior.
methodology: Narrative review/overview chapter (NBER), abstract-only detail on specific effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Offers a broad, consumer-finance-wide (not solely employer-plan) synthesis of when choice-architecture interventions like defaults and product design help or hurt, giving the team a framework for weighing the enrolment and level decisions against the wider behavioral evidence base.
limitations: broad overview rather than a focused study of round-up savings or app-based defaults
abstract gives no concrete effect sizes
covers many topics beyond enrolment defaults, diluting direct applicability
relevance_reason: The kind of review/meta-level synthesis the brief asks for, and it explicitly extends choice-architecture findings beyond employer retirement plans into general household finance.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially anchored on the low default savings rate (2-3%) and default conservative fund, with half still doing so after three years, roughly offsetting participation gains against under-saving from the low default rate.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking automatic-enrollment 401(k) participants over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a preset default level anchors most users for years, directly warning that whichever multiplier (1x/2x/5x) is pre-selected for round-ups will likely become the de facto ceiling for most users rather than a mere starting point.
limitations: employer-mediated retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer app
locked long-term savings vehicle, unlike liquid round-up savings
predates current fintech/EU regulatory context by two decades
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring-on-default-level evidence the newer consumer-fintech literature builds on and argues with, directly relevant to the level-design decision.
